slides.title: The Optical Illusion Of Cheap Shares
slides.card_text: Retail investors routinely confuse share price with company valuation. Buying a stock under ₹200 like Castrol or NHPC feels accessible, but nominal price reveals nothing about valuation. Market cap and P/E ratio determine real equity value, not arbitrary unit pricing.

slides.title: How Nominal Price Anchors Retail
slides.card_text: Analysts promote sub-₹200 targets because psychological price anchoring drives high retail volume. Small-lot buyers rush in thinking a ₹150 share is cheap, ignoring that bloated debt and stagnant earnings make it far more expensive than a ₹3,000 compounder.

slides.title: Creating Necessary Exit Liquidity
slides.card_text: Institutional desks require immense volume to offload large positions without crashing bid prices. Promoting low-priced stock calls generates retail order flow, effectively using uninformed capital as exit liquidity while institutions hedge downside risk around key levels like 55,500.

slides.title: The Real Cost Of Bad Asymmetry
slides.card_text: Tight stop-losses on speculative sub-₹200 calls frequently trigger during noise, compounding transaction friction. A portfolio hit with sequential 5% stop-outs requires an exponential 11.1% gain just to recover capital, permanently destroying long-term compounding velocity.

slides.title: The Valuation Over Price Rule
slides.card_text: Never evaluate equity based on unit share cost. Before taking any technical trade, calculate total Market Cap, P/E ratio relative to sector peers, and institutional ownership trends. Price is merely what you pay; fundamental value is what you actually acquire.

slides.title: The 3-Point Trade Verification Audit
slides.card_text: Before entering low-nominal trades: First, check if Market Cap matches earnings growth. Second, verify if institutional holdings are increasing or dumping. Third, ensure risk-reward asymmetry exceeds 1:3 beyond structural market noise and volatility triggers.
